title: Trump’s approval rating hits all-time low in New Hampshire, UNH poll finds - WCAX
content:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - President Trump’s approval rating is at an all-time low in New Hampshire. That’s according to a new poll from the UNH Survey Center. The data shows that since this summer, fewer people than ever approve of Trump’s performance as president. In 2018, 41% of people strongly approved of Trump’s job as president. By July of this year, only 24% of respondents strongly approved. That number dropped to 22% in August and then 19% in September. It is now at its lowest point in either of Trump’s terms in office. Overall, 67% of New Hampshire residents disapprove of Trump’s overall job as president, only 32% approve, and 1% are unsure. The poll also sheds light on how Granite Staters feel about the Iran conflict. Overall, 75% of respondents think it’s going poorly. Only 23% of people think it’s going well. title: Did UnitedHealth Name The Fix Before Its Stock Ran? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) stock has risen about 40% since late March 2026, against close to 19% for the S&P 500. Read cold, that looks like a recovery nobody could have timed. It was not hidden. The company had said plainly, months before the shares turned, that it would give up members to rebuild margin. In July 2025 the company said its 2026 pricing was built around margin recovery, and it named the bill. It would exit plans serving over 600,000 members, mostly less managed products such as PPO offerings. It was narrowing its Medicare Advantage networks. There was a lot to recover. As of fiscal Q4 2025, the last set of results filed before the run began, UnitedHealth’s trailing-twelve-month operating margin was 4.2%, against a three-year average of 7.8%. Revenue over the same twelve months still grew 11.8%, showing volume and demand remained intact. The problem was that medical costs severely outpaced premiums—pricing had failed to keep up with trend. By October 2025 the company said the repricing at UnitedHealthcare was on track to lift that business’s 2026 operating earnings through margin improvement. In January 2026 it sized the retreat: Medicare Advantage membership would contract by 1.3 million to 1.4 million across 2026, an approach it said favored margin recovery. It was also targeting operating cost reductions of nearly $1 billion. It has. Adjusted earnings per share in fiscal Q2 2026 were $6.38, against $4.08 a year earlier. In July 2026, with the run already under way, it raised its full-year 2026 adjusted earnings outlook to a range of $19.50 to $20 a share. In January 2026 that outlook had been greater than $17.75. Revenue in fiscal Q2 2026 was largely consistent with the prior year, so the improvement did not come from selling more. The payoff came largely from the levers the plan laid out, alongside operational adjustments like benefit design and care management, with the final figures landing better than anticipated. Medicare medical cost growth for 2026 is now expected to land below the initial estimate of around 10%. Management attributes that partly to its own benefit design, care management and network curation. The membership bill came in lighter too: Medicare Advantage enrollment is now expected to fall by about 1.1 million for 2026, against the 1.3 million to 1.4 million it had planned. Partly. The plan was legible and the timing was not. Implied volatility on UNH options climbed from the 37th percentile of its trailing one-year range in early February 2026 to the 91st by mid-March. That said a large move was coming in either direction, and nothing about which one. The reward was not UnitedHealth’s alone either. Elevance Health (ELV) returned 40.3%, a shade ahead of UnitedHealth’s 40.0%, while CVS Health (CVS) returned 24.0% and Cigna (CI) 5.9% over the same window, so reading this plan early bought no more than owning the closest peer did. What the plan has still not fixed is the commercial book, where management now expects full margin recovery to run past 2027. That is what is left to watch, and our guidance momentum screen is where the next company to move its outlook will show up. Perhaps, but you would be paying for a repair that has already happened. The plan is no longer news and what is left is execution on the commercial book. Before you pay up for one company’s turn, see how the rest of the group screens on the same question. Healthcare insurers are navigating a shifting cost environment while balancing membership trends, pricing discipline and the need to improve care delivery efficiency. These factors are placing greater emphasis on how managed care companies manage medical costs and allocate resources across government-sponsored and commercial businesses. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated UNH and Molina Healthcare, Inc. MOH both operate in managed care, but their business models have different levels of diversification. UNH combines UnitedHealthcare with its broad Optum platform spanning care delivery, technology, analytics and pharmacy services, while MOH remains more concentrated in government-sponsored healthcare, particularly Medicaid, Medicare and Marketplace programs. Let's dive deep and closely compare the fundamentals of the two stocks to determine which one is a better investment now. UnitedHealth's earnings recovery is increasingly being driven by better economics at UnitedHealthcare rather than pure membership expansion. The second-quarter medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4% a year earlier, aided by pricing discipline, benefit redesign, business mix and medical cost initiatives. UnitedHealthcare generated revenues of $86 billion in the second quarter of 2026, while operating income climbed to $3.9 billion from $2.1 billion a year ago. Technology is another important efficiency lever for UnitedHealthcare. The business is using digital tools and automation to simplify claims processing, prior authorization, benefit administration and member navigation, helping reduce administrative friction and improve service delivery. Its operating margin improved to 4.6% in the second quarter of 2026 from 2.4% a year ago, despite membership pressure in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid. Optum Health remains a key long-term growth pillar as UnitedHealth expands value-based care and shifts more treatment toward lower-cost settings. Its integrated care model combines physician services, ambulatory care and home-based programs, giving the company opportunities to improve outcomes while reducing unnecessary hospital utilization. Optum is also extending home-based care in rural markets, where it already reaches nearly 90% of U.S. counties and conducts about 2.5 million rural patient home visits annually. Optum Rx and Optum Insight further diversify UnitedHealth beyond traditional health insurance. The company is expanding transparent pharmacy arrangements, healthcare analytics and technology solutions for payers and providers. Together, these businesses give UNH several avenues for growth while reducing its dependence on any single managed-care market. In the second quarter of 2026, Optum's adjusted operating margin improved to 6.1% from 4.6% a year ago. UNH beat earnings in each of the past four quarters with an average surprise of 12.1%. UnitedHealth Group Incorporated price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | UnitedHealth Group Incorporated Quote UNH also maintains a relatively solid financial position. It ended the June quarter with $31.5 billion in cash and short-term investments, sufficient to cover its short-term borrowings and current maturities of long-term debt, which stand at $3.8 billion. Its total debt-to-capital of 41.2% is below MOH's 48.7% and the industry's 41.5%. This balance-sheet flexibility supports continued investment in technology, care delivery and other strategic initiatives. Medicaid remains the foundation of Molina Healthcare's business and a key source of its expected earnings recovery. Medicaid generated $8 billion of premium revenues in the second quarter of 2026. Medical cost trends remained stable, and MOH expects Medicaid margins to improve as future rate increases better reflect underlying cost trends. The company views 2026 as the trough year for Medicaid profitability. Medicare is also becoming a key growth and earnings contributor, particularly through dual-eligible products. The segment's second-quarter MCR was 90.7%, driven by lower medical cost trends in several categories and pricing implemented for 2026. The company plans to exit its traditional Medicare Advantage Part D (MAPD) business in 2027 and direct resources toward integrated plans serving members eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid. This initiative should create a more focused Medicare portfolio while supporting deeper penetration in existing markets. Contract wins and renewals remain central to MOH's growth strategy. The company continues to defend existing Medicaid franchises while pursuing new state contracts and opportunities in integrated dual-eligible programs. This approach provides a path to expand its membership and premium base. Molina Healthcare is also using portfolio discipline and operating leverage to support longer-term growth. It is reducing Marketplace exposure while allocating resources toward Medicaid, Medicare duals and selective acquisitions. The company continues to target $64 billion of premium revenues by 2029. Molina Healthcare is also investing in technology and AI to improve operating efficiency and medical-cost management. The company has migrated to a cloud-based architecture and is using analytics to generate insights for members and state partners. Its AI initiatives are aimed at automating administrative processes and improving managed-care operations. Molina Healthcare also exited the second quarter of 2026 with cash and cash equivalents of $5 billion, which increased from the 2025-end level of $4.2 billion, providing flexibility for acquisitions and other strategic investments. However, it missed the earnings estimates in two of the past four quarters and beat twice. Molina Healthcare, Inc price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Molina Healthcare, Inc Quote The Zacks Consensus Estimate for UNH's 2026 EPS is pegged at $19.85, indicating 21.4% year-over-year growth. The same for 2027 earnings suggests a 13.6% increase to $22.55 per share. Meanwhile, the consensus estimate for 2026 revenues is pegged at $446.8 billion. The consensus mark for Molina Healthcare's 2026 EPS is pegged at $5.29, a 52% decrease from a year ago. However, the same for 2027 predicts an 84.6% rise to $9.76. Meanwhile, the consensus estimate for 2026 revenues is pegged at $44.5 billion. The sharp projected earnings rebound suggests stronger recovery potential for MOH, making its long-term growth outlook appear more compelling compared with UNH. Coming to the valuation story, it seems that investors are willing to pay a premium for Molina Healthcare compared to UnitedHealth. This is reflected in MOH's forward 12-month price/earnings (P/E) of 22.37X compared with UNH's 17.10X and the industry average of 15.21X. In the past three months, shares of UnitedHealth have fallen 8.1% compared with Molina Healthcare's 5.1% decline and the industry's 4.6% dip. During this time, the S&P 500 has risen 5.2%. UNH offers greater diversification through UnitedHealthcare and Optum, supported by improving profitability and a stronger balance sheet. However, membership pressure and the ongoing recovery in its core insurance business remain key considerations. Meanwhile, MOH offers a more focused recovery story, supported by stabilizing Medicaid economics, growth in Medicare duals, new contract wins and a leaner Marketplace portfolio. Despite its higher valuation, its stronger projected earnings rebound makes MOH the more attractive stock at present. Wall Street is navigating a mixed session in which enthusiasm around artificial intelligence remains visible, while oil prices, Treasury yields and geopolitical headlines continue to influence positioning. That divergence has made company-level fundamentals more important, as investors look past broad index moves to identify which businesses can hold up if conditions change. UnitedHealth Group operates UnitedHealthcare, which provides health insurance through employer, individual, Medicare and Medicaid plans, and Optum, which includes care delivery, pharmacy benefit management and health technology. This combination gives it a large presence across the US healthcare system. In 2025, the company faced rising medical costs, especially in Medicare Advantage, which led to reduced profit forecasts and a leadership change, with Stephen Hemsley returning as chief executive. The market is watching whether UnitedHealth can restore profitability through pricing, benefit changes and cost management. Government reimbursement rates for Medicare Advantage, regulatory investigations and policy changes affecting pharmacy benefit managers are also important factors. Healthcare stocks are often considered defensive, but the sector faces significant policy uncertainty. US drug pricing initiatives, tariff discussions on pharmaceuticals and changes to Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement affect drugmakers and insurers. Obesity treatments have become a major growth area, while patent expirations on major drugs push companies to invest in pipelines and acquisitions. Health insurers have faced rising medical costs, which has pressured margins. Clinical trial results and regulatory decisions remain key catalysts for individual stocks. Investors in healthcare track clinical trial data, FDA approvals, product launches, patent expirations and pricing developments. For insurers, the medical cost ratio, enrolment and government reimbursement rates are key. For medical device companies, procedure volumes and new product adoption matter. The Inflation Reduction Act has introduced Medicare drug price negotiations, adding another factor for drugmakers. Mergers and licensing deals remain common as companies seek to replenish pipelines. The broader macro environment adds context for UnitedHealth Group. Interest rates remain a central factor, as changes in bond yields affect borrowing costs, consumer demand and equity valuations. Oil price movements feed into inflation and can shift sector preferences quickly. Meanwhile, the AI spending boom continues to redirect capital across the market, creating both opportunities and competitive pressures. For UnitedHealth Group, these forces shape the operating environment even when the company itself has no major announcements. Optum has three main parts: Optum Health, which runs clinics and provides value-based care; Optum Insight, which provides data analytics and technology to healthcare providers and payers; and Optum Rx, one of the largest pharmacy benefit managers in the US. This vertical integration has been a source of strength but has also drawn scrutiny from regulators and lawmakers. UnitedHealth has also faced a cyberattack at Change Healthcare, a Justice Department investigation into its Medicare billing practices, and public criticism over claims denials. The company suspended its full-year guidance in 2025 and has since worked to reset expectations, raise premiums and adjust benefits in its Medicare Advantage plans. Investor sentiment toward UnitedHealth Group can change quickly as new information emerges. Earnings reports, management commentary, analyst updates and industry news all play a role. As with any listed company, UnitedHealth Group faces risks that could affect its performance. Execution on strategic priorities and the ability to manage costs in an uncertain market will also influence results. title: UNH School of Nursing Earns Top 100 National Ranking - University of New Hampshire
content: The University of New Hampshire School of Nursing’s undergraduate program is among the top 100 in the country, according to U.S. News & World Report. UNH’s program ranked No. 94 on the 2027 U.S. News & World Report Best Colleges Undergraduate Nursing rankings, tied with multiple schools — a significant jump from No. 135 last year. The program’s rise to the top 100 follows a year of growing interest and momentum. More than 2,000 students applied for 120 projected spots in this fall’s incoming class, a 20% increase from the previous year. Demand was so strong that the program reached capacity before UNH’s May 1 enrollment deposit deadline. "We are so proud of our nation-leading School of Nursing. This rise in rankings and recognition as a top 100 school, reflects our nursing faculty's innovative pedagogy, transformative nursing science, and our partnerships across our state and region for world-class clinical learning opportunities,” says Kirsten Corazzini, dean of the College of Health and Human Services (CHHS). “Above all, this ranking exemplifies the UNH nurse who is leading care and creating new ways to support human health and well-being.” From interdisciplinary learning opportunities at the Health Sciences Simulation Center to clinical experiences with UNH’s network of healthcare partners, students have multiple opportunities to gain hands-on experience while making a meaningful impact in communities across the state. The program’s restructuring into the School of Nursing in 2025 also gives undergraduates a clearer path to continue their education at UNH by bringing undergraduate and graduate nursing programs under one unified structure. The school serves approximately 800 students in programs ranging from pre-licensure nursing through clinical doctoral education, including multiple nurse practitioner tracks, with offerings in-person and online. “We’re proud to be recognized in the ranking and excited about the opportunities for current and future students at UNH,” says Rhonda Board, director of nursing. “Our programs provide students with a strong foundation for entering the nursing profession and pathways to continue their education as their goals evolve, whether that means advanced clinical practice, leadership, research, or other areas of nursing. We want UNH to be a place where nurses can continue to learn and grow throughout their careers.” Earlier this year, UNH’s online graduate nursing program rose nearly 70 spots to No. 56 nationally in U.S. News & World Report’s 2026 Best Online Programs rankings. title: Can UNH Stock Keep Growing Earnings While Its Sales Stall? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) has turned its profits around. Operating earnings rose 55% in the second quarter of 2026, and management raised its full-year adjusted earnings guide to $19.50 to $20 a share. Revenue, though, has nearly stopped growing. So the rest of the recovery rests on something the company only partly controls: the medical bills of the people it insures. The rebound came from repricing, not from growth. Year-over-year revenue growth ran above 12% for two quarters, then slowed to 2.0% and to 0.4% in the latest quarter. Second-quarter revenue of $112 billion was largely in line with a year earlier, yet operating earnings grew to $8 billion. Management credits the pricing, benefit design and market actions it has taken over the past year. Medicare Advantage membership is shrinking as well, and the company expects that enrollment to fall by about 1.1 million in 2026. With sales this flat, earnings per share grow only if margins widen or the share count falls. Management still stands by a long-term earnings growth rate of 13% to 16%, and the CEO says that rate includes productivity gains and use of capital. Margin is exactly where the pressure sits. In commercial plans, medical cost trend is running modestly above 11%, and management says it sees no evidence of moderation yet. One primary driver, by the company’s own account, is the arbitration process under the No Surprises Act, which applies only to commercial plans. Management says that process adds about 50 basis points of extra trend in 2026. When arbiters side with out-of-network providers, the average payout is now 11 times what Medicare would pay. Management says the sticky trend is pushing full commercial margin recovery past 2027. Medicare looks better, with trend below plan. Yet management says that is not an inflection point: trend there is continuing at high levels, and its 2027 planning expects no meaningful let-up. In Medicaid, rate increases of around 6% to 7% are still lagging medical trend. Worried enough to watch closely. UnitedHealth can keep growing earnings on flat sales only while its pricing stays ahead of medical cost trend, and in commercial plans that trend shows no sign of easing yet. Management calls the commercial repair a multi-year journey, so this risk will not arrive as one bad headline. Instead, it plays out gradually as contracts reprice against claims. The starting point also had help. Second-quarter results included $860 million of net favorable prior-period medical development, about a tenth of that quarter’s operating earnings. Most of that reserve adjustment stemmed from earlier quarters in 2026 rather than from prior years. Management says the $19.50 to $20 guide is still the right base even though it reflects that development, and that nothing needs carving out. The numbers to watch arrive with third-quarter 2026 results: whether commercial cost trend is still above 11%, and the fresh Medicare trend estimate management has said will probably come then. Options traders are not pricing unusual stress for now, with implied volatility in the 40th percentile of its past year. That depends on what else you hold, because a cost problem like this one surfaces quietly, one report at a time. title: UNH Named Best Value Public University in New England for Sixth Consecutive Year - University of New Hampshire
content: The University of New Hampshire has once again earned the designation of No. 1 best value public university in New England, according to U.S. News & World Report, marking the sixth consecutive year that UNH landed in the top spot in the region. UNH also climbed seven positions from last year to rank No. 50 among top public schools nationally, tied with UC Boulder, UC Santa Cruz, and the University of Tennessee. Additionally, the School of Nursing’s undergraduate program reached the top 100 in the country, vaulting 41 positions from last year to No. 94. The distinctions are part of the 2027 U.S. News & World Report Best College rankings, released Sept. 22. Extending its streak of consecutive years as the top value public university in New England to six is a reflection of UNH’s dedication to providing students the biggest return on their investment, something that becomes more and more important as demographic changes decrease the number of students attending college. “Our goal for New Hampshire’s public research university is to make an excellent education attainable and deliver value that lasts well beyond graduation,” says UNH President Elizabeth Chilton. “That means helping students afford their education, giving them meaningful opportunities to learn through experience and preparing them to succeed in their careers.” Virtually all first-year UNH students – 96% – received scholarships and/or need-based aid this year, and the university just awarded a record $40 million in financial aid to incoming students, with the average student award topping $16,918, a 34% increase from last year. Additionally, the first-year retention rate was 88% last year, well above the national average of 78%. UNH’s four-year graduation rate of 78% also outpaced the national average (59%). Beyond financial assistance, UNH students have access to a wealth of hands-on experience, with 72% of students completing at least one internship before graduation, according to a First Destination survey of 2025 graduates. That same survey showed that 94% of 2025 graduates were employed or seeking further education within six months of graduation, and that the vast majority of employed graduates – 88% – had earned jobs in fields related to their major. UNH has continued to expand the variety of differentiating programs available to students in recent years, launching the Hamel Honors & Scholars College in 2024 and unveiling the School of Nursing within the College of Health and Human Services (CHHS) in 2025. That preceded the climb of more than 40 spots in the rankings for UNH’s undergraduate nursing program, from No. 135 in 2026 to No. 94 this year. title: Remembering the UNH community members lost during 9/11 - tnhdigital.com
content: On September 11th, 2001, tragedy struck as the twin towers fell in a terrorist attack against the United States. 2,996 people lost their lives that day, including mothers, spouses, and children. 247 passengers boarded the four planes: American Airlines Flight 11, United Airlines Flight 175, American Airlines Flight 77, and United Airlines Flight 93. Among the victims of this tragedy, four were University of New Hampshire (UNH) alumni. Although they came from different backgrounds and had different experiences at UNH, each person left an important impact on their friends, family, and the UNH community. Judd Cavalier `98 was a beloved member of the Sigma Beta fraternity and was known for being the “house chef.” In 1996, Cavalier took a semester off and found his passion for sales in the Rocky Mountains selling ski equipment. Cavalier was known for acquiring a pool table for him and his roommates.  When Cavalier graduated in 1998, he donated his pool table to the Sigma Beta house, where it remains to this day. During the summer of 1996, Cavalier got an internship at Sandler O’Neill and Partners, an investment banking firm in New York City. After graduating, he was asked to come back as a full-time employee. He moved to Long Island with his childhood friend Joseph Anchundia, whom he helped get a position at the same company. On September 11th, 2001, they died together while at work on the 104th floor of South Tower. Jennifer Fialko `94 was a patriotic New Hampshire citizen. Fialko’s mother described her love of the state and drive to attend the University of New Hampshire. Her favorite place to be was waterskiing on Lake Winnipesaukee. Fialko majored in Sociology and was a beloved member of the Sigma Iota Sigma sorority. Her sorority sisters remembered what a great friend Fialko was and how she was always the first one there in times of need. During her junior year at UNH, she studied Spanish and traveled abroad to Granada, Spain. Her passion for languages continued even after graduation, when she traveled to Brazil and learned Portuguese. Two years after Fialko graduated, she was diagnosed with Hodgkin’s Lymphoma. Despite the hardships and challenges, Fialko persisted; she went through rounds of chemotherapy, developing her own essential oil business to combat the side effects of chemotherapy. In August 2001, Fialko was offered a position at Aon, a client-service insurance company located in the South Tower of the World Trade Center. On September 11th, 2001, Fialko was working on the 92nd floor when the second plane struck. Timothy Stout `83 was described as a dependable and enthusiastic man. He was a member of the UNH Crew team and lived in the crew house with his friends and teammates. described as someone who gave his 100% and someone you always wanted around. His mother described him as a good and kind man, taking on responsibilities such as doing the laundry, grilling and cooking for the family, playing with the kids, and making them popcorn. He fell in love with and married Maryellen Fanelli in 1991. Together they had three kids: Timothy Jr., now 32 (7 at the time), Matthew, now 30 (5 at the time), and Shannon, now 29 (4 at the time). After their father had died, his kids made a list of the top 10 things they had loved about their dad, which is now on the 9/11 Memorial website: He had found a career at the global financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald. On September 11th, 2001, he had been on the 103rd floor of the North Tower when the first plane struck. Robert LeBlanc, '59, a UNH alum and geography professor, was a favorite professor of many UNH students. He graduated from Nashua High School in 1930 and enlisted in the Air Force, from which he was discharged in 1953. As a student at UNH, LeBlanc studied geologist Donald H. Chapman’s work on glacial studies in the Arctic. LeBlanc himself was Franco-American and invested in his heritage and loved travel, culture, and language. LeBlanc and his wife had tickets and plans to go to Argentina, India, and Sweden in the near future. After his death, his wife joked that he had so many frequent flyer miles from multiple airlines that she couldn’t even sort them all. On September 11th, 2001, he boarded United Airlines Flight 175 on his way to a geology conference in Los Angeles. September 11th, 2001, is a day to be remembered and to mourn those who were lost; those who sacrificed their lives to save others, and those who worked in the 170 hospitals and triage centers that cared for and aided victims that day. It is important to continue to honor all those who were lost.

title: Crimson Football: Harvard 31, UNH 7 - Harvard Magazine
content:
Your independent source for Harvard news since 1898 Football



					|
				
			September 21, 2026 TACKLING TWINS Harvard linebackers Sean Line (35) and Dorsey Benefield led the defensive charge for the Crimson. | Photograph courtesy of Harvard Athletics Communications Welcome back! After a 41-week break for irrelevant activities such as exams, theses, and Commencement, Harvard football returned on Saturday. To kick off its 152nd season, the Crimson ventured to Wildcat Stadium in Durham, New Hampshire, to take on the University of New Hampshire. Harvard emerged with a solid 31-7 victory that contained one big asterisk (more on that later). With Stephenson family head coach for Harvard football Andrew Aurich entering his third season, the Crimson are hoping to win a fourth straight Ivy title—they have been co-champions for three years—and venture to the Football Championship Subdivision (FCS) postseason for a second consecutive year. The voters in the Ivy League’s media preseason poll were somewhat bullish on the Crimson’s chances, picking them to finish second, albeit way behind last year’s co-champion Yale. Join thousands of readers getting the news, ideas, and conversations shaping Harvard—every Friday. Free. No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.
Privacy policy. HARVARD FOOTBALLSign up for Harvard Magazine’s weekly email for Dick Friedman's football recaps in your inbox every Friday. Saturday’s victory was largely attributable to the Harvard defense. The Crimson sacked New Hampshire quarterback Brooks Bentley seven times, picked off two passes, and, acting like Horatius at the bridge, stymied the Wildcats five times on fourth down, once at the Crimson one-yard line. Marauding senior linebacker Sean Line (a game-high 10 tackles, 3.5 for loss, two sacks) and his compatriot, junior Dorsey Benefield (eight tackles), were wherever a Wildcat ballcarrier was. On Monday, Line was named Ivy League defensive player of the week. On offense, as has been the case since time immemorial, Harvard has uncovered a fleet of promising running backs to supplement senior captain Xaviah Bascon (54 yards on 15 carries, one touchdown). The prominent newcomers include sophomore Cole Allen (62 yards on 12 carries) and freshman Nathan Bailey (73 all-purpose yards). Working behind a seasoned offensive line, they were able to keep the Crimson moving. As for the asterisk? It related to the biggest question of the off-season: who would replace All-Ivy Jaden Craig as quarterback? The player who emerged was sophomore Charlie Smith, who won the starting job over senior Dante Torres. Alas, Smith’s debut was a shaky shakedown cruise. He had 11 completions in 19 pass attempts for a mere 71 yards, with one touchdown and one interception. Most of the time Smith was inaccurate and struggled to find his receivers. On Saturday, at least, the rest of the offense picked him up. The game was scoreless until early in the second quarter. Then, Bailey took a punt and returned it for 28 yards to the New Hampshire 32. On first down, senior running back Jordan Harris bounced outside for a 25-yard gain. Four plays later, freshman wildcat formation quarterback Kise Flannery scored the first touchdown of the year on a one-yard run. (The wildcat formation is one in which a predominantly running quarterback is inserted.) Junior placekicker Kieran Corr banged the season’s first extra point through the uprights. Harvard 7, New Hampshire 0. The Wildcats responded immediately. On the next series, Bentley found wide receiver Ty Carlson all alone down the middle for a 40-yard gain. Six plays later, Bentley surged into the end zone from the one-yard line. Lucas Glassburn converted. Harvard 7, New Hampshire 7. At the end of the half, the Crimson took command. With just under three minutes to go, Allen rushed five times for 24 yards. Then, from the New Hampshire 23, a reverse: Smith took the snap, headed left—and pitched to Bailey coming the other way. With the Wildcats fooled by the misdirection, Bailey had a clear path to ease into the end zone. Corr kicked. Harvard 14, New Hampshire 7. Fifty-three seconds remained in the half. The Wildcats tried to take advantage of the time that was left. It backfired. Bentley tossed a pass that Crimson junior defensive back D.J. Vincent-Thomas picked off and returned 30 yards to the New Hampshire 13. On the next play, Smith found Bailey in the end zone. Corr booted. Harvard 21, New Hampshire 7. In the third quarter, the Wildcats tried to get back in the game. After Smith threw an interception, New Hampshire drove to the Harvard 10. On fourth and inches, the Crimson defense stuffed Bentley. Harvard took over and kept the ball for 13 plays, culminating in a 24-yard Corr field goal. Harvard 24, New Hampshire 7. At this point the result was hardly in doubt, but the game was salted away after a poor Wildcat punt gave the Crimson the ball at the New Hampshire 25. Smith threw his best pass of the day, to junior running back Maddux Reid at the 10. Reid toted the ball to the three. Two plays later Bascon scored from the one. Corr punctuated. Harvard 31, New Hampshire 7. The Crimson are now 1-0, as they always seem to be at this juncture (see below). New Hampshire, which plays in the Colonial Athletic Association, was already playing its fourth game of the season, and dropped to 1-3. No rest for the weary: the first Ivy game of the year, at Brown, awaits on Friday night. FOR OPENERS: Saturday’s victory was Harvard’s sixth in a row on opening day. It also ran the Crimson’s all-time mark in season openers to 125-25-2. Which is to say, Harvard could lose the next 100 openers and still be at .500. GRAD MADNESS: With rules now permitting graduates to play an additional year of college football, three prominent members of the Harvard Class of 2026 have landed at Football Bowl Subdivision schools: quarterback Jaden Craig at Texas Christian University (TCU), receiver Cooper Barkate at the University of Miami, and safety Ty Bartrum at the University of Central Florida (UCF). This coming Saturday, Craig and Bartrum will be looking at each other across the line of scrimmage when TCU travels to Orlando, Florida, to face UCF. A harmonic (or not so) convergence! HELLO, GOOD BYE: Beginning in the 2027 season, the Ivy League will adopt a midseason bye. In ’27, the time off will occur the weekend of October 23 (formally, Week 7 of the season), which would have been the date of the Princeton game. To maintain the pre-Thanksgiving finish to the season, the opener will be on September 11—one week earlier than in recent years—with the Crimson leaping right into the Ivy cauldron, traveling to New Jersey to tussle with the Tigers.BOZEMAN, HERE WE COME: To enlarge its football footprint (and mindful of potential playoff seeding), in the coming years Harvard will roam far afield to battle traditional FCS powers. In 2027, the Crimson will host University of California, Davis, a playoff quarterfinalist last year, and in 2031 Harvard will journey to California for a return match. In 2028, Harvard will travel to Bozeman, Montana, to take on rugged Montana State, the current reigning FCS champion. That season the Crimson will also host Wofford. In 2031 and 2032, Harvard will play a home-and-home series with Richmond. All will be first-time opponents. COMING UP: On Friday evening, Harvard journeys to Providence to play its Ivy opener against Brown. Kickoff: 7 p.m. The game will be telecast on ESPN2 and broadcast on radio at Bloomberg 92.9 FM and WHRB 95.3 FM. In a series that began in 1893, the Crimson lead 91-31-2. content: U.S. stock futures traded lower late Monday as traders tracked U.S. President Donald Trump’s deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while weighing ceasefire talks amid elevated oil prices. As of 10.15 p.m. ET, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures were down by 0.6%. Dow futures were down 0.4%. Speaking at a White House conference on Monday, Trump reiterated that the U.S. military could target Iranian bridges and power plants if the strait is not reopened by 8 p.m. ET Tuesday. He said negotiations were “going well,” but added that restoring access through Hormuz remains a “very big priority.” He also said that while he would like the U.S. to “take the oil,” Americans ultimately want U.S. forces to return home. The U.S., Iran and regional mediators are reportedly exploring a possible 45-day ceasefire that could open the door to a settlement, while Washington and Tehran are also supposedly reviewing a Pakistan-brokered proposal to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. However, Tehran has said it would only accept ceasefire terms that include a permanent end to the war, sanctions relief, reconstruction commitments and guarantees around safe navigation through the strait. It also warned that strikes on civilian infrastructure could trigger retaliatory attacks on energy facilities across the Gulf. The conflict, now in its sixth week, continues to ripple through energy markets, with West Texas Intermediate settling near $112.41 per barrel and Brent crude closing around $109.77. Michael Cembalest, chair of market and investment strategy at J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management, said that the belief the U.S. economy is insulated from a closure of the Strait of Hormuz is “mostly false,” adding that U.S. fossil-fuel independence “is not as much of an economic firewall as you might think.” In the previous session, the S&P 500 logged its fourth straight session of gains, marking its longest winning streak since January: Investors also weighed weaker-than-expected economic data, with the U.S. services sector expanding at a slower pace in March. The ISM services index fell 2.1 points to 54, with employment posting its sharpest drop since 2023. Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, said on X that the report “reinforces the dual narrative of rising input prices and a resilient real economy.” Avis Budget Group (CAR): Shares hit nearly a three-year high on Monday despite Deutsche Bank downgrading the stock to 'Hold,' saying the recent 30% weekly rally appears driven by technical reasons tied to a potential short squeeze rather than fundamentals. Broadcom (AVGO): Shares rose 2% in extended trading after the company announced a long-term agreement with Alphabet’s Google to develop and supply next-generation Tensor Processing Units and expand AI infrastructure partnership through 2031 alongside Anthropic. Enovix (ENVX): Shares posted their best session in nine months on Monday as retail traders speculated about a potential catalyst after Chinese media reported a deal with AR-optics firm MoJie to improve battery life in AI-enabled smart glasses. Humana (HUM), UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Elevance Health (ELV): Shares of health insurers rallied in extended trading after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, expected to add more than $13 billion in plan funding. In broader markets, the yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note hovered near 4.33%, its highest level in about a week. Gold steadied near $4,664 per ounce after a two-day slide, while silver traded around $73.18. (TSLA) flashed fresh warning signals on Monday after slipping below key levels following a first-quarter (Q1) delivery miss, with one analyst projecting nearly 40% downside by June as bearish calls built after JPMorgan flagged a major downside to the stock. TSLA stock fell more than 2% on Monday, marking its lowest level in nearly seven months. GLJ Research analyst Gordon Johnson said on X that Tesla has broken below its 20, 50 and 75-day moving averages and remains trapped in a descending channel that began after the stock’s December highs near $480. He added that Fibonacci levels point to $322 as the next key support, while momentum indicators indicate the stock is not yet oversold. Johnson said investors should watch the $322- $346 range for a potential bounce. The analyst also said that, assuming consensus expectations for negative $1.6 billion in first-quarter free cash flow prove accurate and that prior correlations between Tesla’s free cash flow performance and its share price continue to hold, the stock could fall to $224-$269 by June 30, implying a 24%-36% downside from current levels. He also noted that Tesla’s car sales declined year-over-year in both 2024 and 2025 and are expected to fall again in 2026. “$TSLA has made literally NO PROGRESS on ‘robotaxis’ since launching in Austin in June of last yr. It could fall another 70-80%, and STILL be massively overvalued,” Johnson said, adding that the stock trades as 288x estimated 2026 earnings versus 31x for the Magnificent Seven. Johnson’s technical warning follows a bearish update from JPMorgan analyst Ryan Brinkman, who reiterated an ‘Underweight’ rating and set a $145 price target after Tesla’s Q1 delivery report, implying a 60% downside to current levels. “We ... advise investors approach TSLA shares with a high degree of caution,” Brinkman said. He also lowered 2026 earnings per share (EPS) estimate to $1.8 from $2, below consensus expectations, citing risks to demand, execution and competition as Tesla expands into lower-priced, higher-volume vehicle segments. Future Fund Managing Partner Gary Black said on X, “TSLA bulls out in full force today attacking Ryan Brinkman the person. Yes he’s been wrong on TSLA for 10 years, but he’s been right on TSLA the past five years, so has some credibility.” Separately, Jim Cramer called the bearish JPMorgan call “bold” and speculated that it “must mean people are going to sell this one to buy SpaceX.” His comment follows reports that SpaceX has confidentially filed for a U.S. initial public offering that could become the largest IPO on record, with the company reportedly valued at about $1.75 trillion. Tesla delivered 358,023 vehicles globally in the first quarter, missing Wall Street expectations for a second straight quarter. Deliveries rose 6% from the previous year but fell 14% from a quarter ago, marking the company’s weakest quarter since 2022 outside a Model Y production adjustment period. The company produced 408,386 vehicles during the quarter. Model 3 and Model Y deliveries totaled 341,893 units, while Model S, Model X and Cybertruck deliveries reached 16,130 units. Tesla also deployed 8.8 gigawatt-hours of energy-storage products, down from 10.4 gigawatt-hours a year earlier and below estimates. The results come as the U.S. electric-vehicle market adjusts to the phase-out of federal purchase incentives and competition from Chinese automakers intensifies across markets. Even as bearish calls emerged after the delivery miss, Baird maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating and lowered its price target to $538 from $548, still implying a 52% upside from the stock’s last close, according to an Investing report. title: UNH Stock Technicals Today: Gains 0.45%, Testing Support Level - JournalArta

On September 21, 2026: price 376.90 USD, trend downtrend, RSI 37.0, support 375.21, resistance 401.01. technical analysis of unh  stock.Dapatkan Kalender Digital UnitedHealth Group shares slipped to 376.90 USD on the NYSE, leaving the stock just above its recent floor and still trading below the short- and medium-term trend lines. The move matters because it shows a large, defensive health-care name is not being treated as a safe haven by the market right now; instead, the chart is still being pulled lower by weak trend structure and negative momentum.Track Business News The stock remains in a downtrend, with the SMA20 at 390.30 and the SMA50 at 404.33 both sitting above the current price. That positioning is important: when price stays below both moving averages, rallies tend to be treated as recovery attempts rather than confirmed trend reversals. The fact that the SMA20 slope is -0.99% over 5 days reinforces that the short-term trend is still leaning lower rather than flattening out.Track Stocks Bonds There is also no fresh moving-average crossover to suggest a new trend regime. In practical terms, that means the chart has not yet produced the kind of technical reset that usually accompanies a durable rebound. The stock is not collapsing in a straight line, but it is still drifting under overhead resistance from its own trend markers. The price is sitting near the lower end of its recent range, with the 20-hour support at 375.21 and 20-hour resistance at 401.01. At 7% of the range, the stock is close to support, which often attracts bargain-hunting interest, but only if buyers can prove they are willing to defend that level. The 3-month low is 372.42, so the market is already operating close to the point where recent selling pressure has previously been absorbed. Momentum is mixed, and that is the key message from the oscillators. The RSI at 37.0 is technically neutral, but it sits close to the lower end of the scale, which tells readers the stock is weak without yet being deeply washed out. By contrast, the Stochastic %K at 13.1 and %D at 7.6 are both in oversold territory. That usually means the stock has been sold aggressively enough that a short-term bounce becomes more likely, but oversold does not automatically mean reversal; it simply means downside momentum may be stretched. The more important caution sign is the MACD at -7.324, still below its signal line at -5.955, with a histogram of -1.368. That combination means downside momentum is still dominating the chart even as some oscillators begin to look tired. In plain language: the stock may be near a short-term bounce zone, but the broader momentum engine has not yet turned positive. Volatility is present, but not extreme. The ATR(14) at 10.20, equal to 2.7% of price, suggests the stock is capable of meaningful daily swings without being in panic mode. That matters because a move through support or resistance is more likely to be followed through when volatility is sufficient to carry price beyond a level, rather than trapping it in a narrow band. The Bollinger setup adds another layer. Price is near the lower band, with the lower Bollinger band at 372.01 and %B at 13%. A low %B means the stock is trading very close to the bottom of its recent volatility envelope, which often reflects either exhaustion selling or the start of a deeper break. The distinction depends on follow-through. Since the Bollinger band width is 9.4% and described as normal, this is not a volatility squeeze that typically precedes a dramatic breakout; it is a standard range where the next move still needs confirmation. Volume, however, is the one area showing real participation. Last session volume was 8,606,300, about 1.7× the 20-day average of 4,950,310. Heavy volume on a weak chart can mean capitulation, but the OBV is falling, which signals that the balance of volume has still been favoring sellers over time. In other words, the market is trading actively, but not yet accumulating the shares in a way that would confirm a durable base. The immediate technical map is clear. The first level to watch is 375.21; that is the nearest support and also the latest reference point for whether buyers can keep the  stock from slipping further. If that area holds, a rebound toward the 390.30 midpoint and then the 401.01 resistance zone becomes the most logical path. If price fails to hold 375.21, the chart risks testing the 372.42 3-month low, which would confirm that the market is still probing for a stronger floor. The upside is capped for now by the SMA20 at 390.30 and then the SMA50 at 404.33. Those levels matter because they are not just arbitrary numbers; they represent where recent buyers have already lost control of the trend. A move back above them would be needed to shift the chart from defensive to constructive. HOLD (wait & see) fits the chart best because the stock is near support and oversold on Stochastic, but the broader trend and MACD remain negative. - Reason 1: The price is still below the SMA20 at 390.30 and SMA50 at 404.33, so the trend has not turned up.
- Reason 2: The MACD is negative and below its signal line, showing downside momentum is still in control.
- Reason 3: Stochastic is oversold and price is near the 375.21 support, which raises the chance of a bounce but does not confirm it. - Verdict invalidated if price breaks below 375.21, because that would expose the 372.42 3-month low and weaken the case for a near-term base.
- Ideal entry range: 375.21 to 372.42, where support and the lower Bollinger band cluster.
- Exit target: 390.30 to 401.01, where the SMA20 and nearby resistance sit.
- Stop loss protection: Below 372.42, if the support shelf fails. For non-traders, this means the stock is close to a possible turning point, but the chart has not yet shown enough strength to say the decline is over. UnitedHealth’s next technical test is whether 375.21 can hold as the market watches the 372.42 low. The English-language global edition of JournalArta.
